# Chapter exercise: Location and Coordinate Systems {.unnumbered}

**Measuring North Carolina**

This exercise goes with **Chapter 12, Location and Coordinate Systems**. It builds on the tmap and geographic data exercises from Chapters 10 and 11. It should take you about **one hour**. Read this whole section before you start.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}

## Purpose

**Skills you'll practice.** By the end of this exercise you will be able to:

1. Calculate the flattening of the ellipsoid, and how long a degree of longitude is at different latitudes.
2. Convert coordinates between degrees, minutes, and seconds (DMS) and decimal degrees, with your own functions.
3. Make an sf layer of points from a table of latitudes and longitudes.
4. Check a layer's coordinate reference system with `st_crs()`, and change it with `st_transform()`.
5. Measure areas and distances in different projections, and explain why the answers differ.
6. Choose a projection for a task.

**Knowledge you'll gain.** You'll measure the area of North Carolina and the distances between five of its cities, and find out how much the map projection on your phone (Web Mercator) exaggerates them.

**Why this matters.** Every spatial layer comes with a coordinate reference system, and every measurement you make (an area, a distance, a buffer, a density) is only as good as the CRS it was calculated in. Mixing up degrees and meters, or measuring on a Web Mercator map, is one of the most common ways a spatial analysis goes quietly wrong. From here on, every NC assignment asks you to project to NC State Plane (EPSG:32119) before measuring anything; this exercise shows you why.

## Task

Work through Parts 1 to 7 in order, top to bottom. In each part:

- Read the short explanation, then do each step marked with a bullet (•).
- Wherever you see `___`, replace it with the missing code **before** you run the chunk. A chunk with `___` in it won't run.
- **Before you run** each chunk, predict roughly what it will return. Then run it and check.
- Answer each question (**Q1**, **Q2**, ...) in a sentence or two of Markdown, where it says *Your answer here.*
- Give every distance and area with its units.

| Part | What you'll do | About |
|:-----|:---------------|:------|
| 1 | Set up your file and load the data | 3 min |
| 2 | The shape of the Earth and the length of a degree | 8 min |
| 3 | Convert between DMS and decimal degrees | 10 min |
| 4 | Make a layer of NC cities | 7 min |
| 5 | Check and change the CRS, and measure area | 12 min |
| 6 | Measure distances | 12 min |
| 7 | Choose a projection, reflect, and turn in | 8 min |

**Turn in** your `.Rmd` file and your knitted `.html` file on Canvas.

## Criteria for success

Use this checklist before you turn your work in. Each item matches a row of the rubric below.

- [ ] The file knits to HTML with no errors, and the author and date at the top are yours.
- [ ] Every `___` has been filled in, and every chunk runs.
- [ ] Your two DMS functions return the test values given in Part 3.
- [ ] Every question (Q1 to Q12) has an answer in complete sentences, with units for every distance and area.
- [ ] You can say which CRS each measurement was made in, and why it does or doesn't distort.
- [ ] Longitudes west of Greenwich are negative.
- [ ] No `install.packages()` line is anywhere in the file.
- [ ] The three reflection questions are answered.

| Criterion | Full credit | Partial credit | No credit |
|:----------|:------------|:---------------|:----------|
| Knits (2 pts) | Knits to HTML with no errors | Knits, but some chunks have errors shown | Doesn't knit, or no HTML turned in |
| Code (5 pts) | Every blank filled in correctly; functions pass their tests | Most blanks correct | Many blanks missing or wrong |
| Questions (9 pts) | Q1 to Q12 answered correctly, with units, naming the CRS, with reasons | Some answers missing, wrong, or without units | Most answers missing |
| Projection choices (2 pts) | Q12 names a sensible projection for each task, with a reason | Some choices without reasons | Not done |
| Style (1 pt) | Readable code, pipe for chains, no `install.packages()` | | Several problems |
| Reflection (1 pt) | All three answered | | Missing |

**What a good answer looks like.** Here is a question, a weak answer, and a strong one.

> *Question:* How far is it from Chapel Hill to Raleigh?
>
> *Weak answer:* "40492."
>
> *Strong answer:* "About 40.5 km (25 miles) in a straight line, measured with `st_distance()` on the WGS84 points. NC State Plane gives the same distance to within 0.1 km, but Web Mercator says 50 km, about 23% too far."

The strong answer gives units, says how the distance was measured, and compares it with the other projections.

**IMPORTANT!** Save often. Before you knit, choose **Run > Restart R and Run All Chunks** to make sure every chunk works from a fresh start.
